story.title: Iran Sets Six Conditions for U.S. to Reopen Strait of Hormuz
story.summary: Iran has outlined six demands that the U.S. must meet to cease attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. In response, President Trump has instructed his representatives to seek reparations from Iran, complicating negotiations further. The exchange of demands has led to rising oil prices and U.S. bond yields, indicating increased market tension.

event_overview.title: About Iran Relations
event_overview.subject: Iran Relations
event_overview.summary: Iran relations in this timeline concern the long-running, largely adversarial relationship between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran, shaped by the absence of formal diplomatic ties, sanctions, nuclear-policy disputes, and security issues in the Persian Gulf. The immediate context also includes the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway between Iran and Oman whose security affects international energy shipments.

facts.label: Diplomatic status
facts.value: The United States severed diplomatic relations with Iran on April 7, 1980; Switzerland serves as the protecting power for U.S. interests in Iran.

facts.label: Nuclear diplomacy framework
facts.value: Iran, China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom, the United States, and the European Union concluded the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) on July 14, 2015. The UN Security Council unanimously endorsed it through Resolution 2231 on July 20, 2015.

facts.label: International nuclear verification
facts.value: Iran's safeguards agreement with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), connected to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, entered into force on May 15, 1974; the IAEA is the international body responsible for applying those safeguards.

facts.label: U.S. economic measures
facts.value: U.S. Iran sanctions are administered and enforced by the Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control under multiple statutes, executive orders, regulations, and, where applicable, UN Security Council measures.

facts.label: Strait of Hormuz
facts.value: The Strait of Hormuz lies between Iran and Oman and connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea, making it a major oil-transit chokepoint.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers specific developments from August 2 through August 11, 2026 involving reported U.S.-Iran diplomacy, military pressure, and Strait of Hormuz access; it does not attempt to cover the full history of U.S.-Iran relations, all nuclear negotiations, sanctions actions, or regional security events.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next procedurally?
explore_lenses.title: Routes may advance before a full deal
explore_lenses.summary: The clearest near-term process is work through intermediaries on limited shipping arrangements, not a confirmed full reopening. That track is occurring alongside incompatible public claims over control of the strait and conditions for ending restrictions.

claims.text: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with Oman on defining new shipping routes was in its final stages, while stressing that this would not itself mean the Strait of Hormuz had reopened.
Araghchi said other conditions had been conveyed to the U.S. through intermediaries, indicating that indirect diplomacy remains the reported channel.

The White House said in July that Trump viewed a deal as possible but asserted U.S. control of the strait and said Iran could still disrupt transit with mines; these are administration claims rather than a jointly accepted account.

Euronews reported that Trump described Washington as only semi-negotiating and willing to allow economic pressure on Iran to continue rather than immediately resume a military campaign; this suggests a slower negotiating approach, not a settled procedure or deadline.

story_report.summary: Iran has set six conditions for the United States to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while President Donald Trump has instructed U.S. representatives to seek reparations from Tehran. The competing demands have complicated indirect negotiations and coincided with higher oil prices and rising U.S. bond yields, signaling increased market tension as the status of transit through the waterway remains unsettled.

sections.heading: Iranian Shipping Route Discussions Continue
sections.body: Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said an agreement with Oman to define new shipping routes was in its final stages. He stressed, however, that such an arrangement would not by itself mean the Strait of Hormuz had reopened. Araghchi also said Iran had conveyed its other conditions to Washington through intermediaries, leaving indirect diplomacy as the reported channel for any broader arrangement.

sections.heading: Trump Administration Maintains Pressure Strategy
sections.body: The White House said in July that Trump believed a deal was possible, while asserting U.S. control of the strait and warning that Iran could still disrupt transit with mines. Those are administration claims rather than a jointly accepted account. Euronews reported that Trump characterized Washington as only semi-negotiating and was prepared to allow economic pressure on Iran to continue rather than immediately resume a military campaign.

unresolved.text: The consulted sources did not identify a verified date for reopening, vessel-eligibility rules, an enforcement arrangement, or a formal agreement providing for full transit through the Strait of Hormuz.
